description: What makes Odysseus a hero — his qualities, flaws, and the Homeric heroic code of kleos, time and endurance.
content_html:
The Homeric Hero

In the world of the Odyssey, a hero is not simply a good person. A hero is someone who achieves great deeds, wins lasting fame, and earns the respect — and fear — of other men. The Homeric concept of heroism is built around two Greek values: kleos (glory) and time (honour). A hero’s kleos is the fame that survives his death, passed on in the songs of bards. His time is the honour shown to him by his community — gifts, prestige, the right to speak first at an assembly. To lose time is a devastating blow; to win kleos is the highest aspiration.

The Iliad, Homer’s other poem, presents the ideal of the warrior-hero most clearly in Achilles: the greatest fighter, whose wrath drives the whole story, who chooses a short glorious life over a long quiet one. Odysseus, by contrast, is a different kind of hero. He is brave and strong, but his defining virtue is intelligence, not brute strength. This creates a fascinating tension: is the cleverest man always the best hero? The Odyssey argues yes — and the prescribed books are Homer’s case for that argument.

Key Fact

Kleos (glory/fame) and time (honour) are the two central heroic values in Homeric epic. Kleos is the lasting fame a hero earns through great deeds — it lives on after death in poetry and song. Time is the immediate respect shown by a community. Losing either is a catastrophe; winning both is the ultimate aspiration.

Odysseus as Leader, Husband and Father

The Odyssey tests Odysseus’s heroism across three roles simultaneously. As a leader, he is responsible for the lives of his crew. He plans carefully, issues orders, and holds his men together in the face of terrifying obstacles. Yet his leadership is not always flawless: his men die, largely because they cannot match his self-restraint. In Book 12, they eat the sacred cattle of the sun god Helios, despite Odysseus’s explicit warnings. They are destroyed as a result. Odysseus’s failure as a leader is that he cannot always prevent his men from being their own worst enemy.

As a husband, Odysseus’s devotion to Penelope is the emotional core of the poem. He refuses the offer of immortality from the goddess Calypso, who holds him on her island for seven years, because he would rather be a mortal man with a wife and a home than an immortal without them. This choice is central to the poem’s values: Odysseus knows what he is and what he values. The home, the marriage bed, the kingdom — these are worth more to him than divine status.

As a father, his relationship with Telemachus is one of the poem’s most moving dimensions. Telemachus is twenty years old; he has grown up without a father. The poem traces his development from a boy who cannot challenge the suitors into a young man who fights alongside his father in Book 22. This growth is partly Athena’s work, but it is also inspired by Odysseus’s own example: when Telemachus sees what his father can do, he finds the courage to act.

Greek epic contrasts two kinds of heroic power. Bie (raw physical force) is the value of Achilles or Heracles — overwhelming strength that defeats enemies directly. Metis (cunning intelligence) is Odysseus’s value — the ability to solve a problem indirectly, through deception, disguise or verbal skill. The Odyssey is, in one sense, a sustained argument that metis is at least as valuable as bie — perhaps more so, since the challenges Odysseus faces cannot be defeated by strength alone.

The Cyclops episode is the clearest example. Polyphemus is vastly stronger than Odysseus and his men. Physical force would be useless. Only metis — the Nobody trick, the stake, the rams — can save them. Similarly, in Book 22 Odysseus does not defeat over a hundred suitors by physical prowess alone: he needs the element of surprise, a secured door, and the help of Athena. The poem suggests that a hero who knows when to use cunning and when to use strength is greater than one who can only do the latter.

The Flaws of Odysseus

Odysseus is not a perfect hero. His most prominent flaw, seen most clearly in the Cyclops episode, is excessive pride — what the Greeks called hubris. After escaping from Polyphemus, Odysseus cannot resist revealing his real name. The boast is humanly understandable — he has just achieved something extraordinary — but it is disastrous in its consequences, setting Poseidon against him for the rest of the poem. A truly wise hero would have stayed silent.

Odysseus also shows a capacity for ruthlessness that can disturb modern readers. He lies freely, to almost everyone he encounters. He shows very little grief for the men he loses. He kills the suitors without giving even the most innocent a chance to escape. Homer does not present these as straightforward virtues; the poem invites the reader to think hard about what kind of man Odysseus is, and whether his ends justify his means. This moral complexity is part of what makes the Odyssey worth studying.

Key Fact

Odysseus’s two most important flaws are pride (hubris — revealed by the boast to Polyphemus, which costs him Poseidon’s enmity) and his capacity for deception (he lies even to loyal characters, including Penelope in Book 19, though this is also what enables his survival). These flaws complicate his heroism without cancelling it.

One of the qualities Homer most praises in Odysseus is endurance — the ability to bear suffering without breaking. This is called karteria. Odysseus weeps for his home regularly, but he never gives up. He endures Calypso’s island for seven years without losing his sense of who he is. He sits in his own palace disguised as a beggar, being mocked and humiliated by the suitors, without revealing himself. This sustained self-control — knowing when to act and when to wait — is what ultimately wins him everything he wants.

This makes Odysseus a quite different kind of hero from Achilles, whose defining choice is to act immediately and violently when his honour is threatened. Odysseus chooses patience over pride (except in the Cyclops episode), strategy over impulse. Whether this makes him a more admirable figure than Achilles is a question the poem raises but does not simply answer — and that open question is ideal material for an essay.

Odysseus’s Relationship with Athena

Throughout the Odyssey, Athena is Odysseus’s protector and closest divine ally. She intervenes at almost every critical moment: she inspires Telemachus to seek news of his father, she engineers Odysseus’s release from Calypso’s island by appealing to Zeus, she gives Odysseus his beggar’s disguise, and she tips the balance of the battle in Book 22. Their relationship is explicitly described as a friendship of equals in intellect: Athena tells Odysseus that she favours him because he is “the cleverest of mortals,” just as she is the cleverest of the gods. This mutual recognition of metis — goddess and man bonded by their shared love of craft and cunning — is one of the most charming ideas in the poem.
exam_tip_html: For questions asking you to evaluate Odysseus as a hero, avoid simply listing his qualities. Examiners want to see you engage with the complexity: what are his strengths, what are his weaknesses, and how does Homer use specific episodes to reveal both? Always name the book and the episode (e.g. ‘in Book 9, his pride when he reveals his name to Polyphemus’). For essay questions that ask ‘how far do you agree,’ you must present both sides: the case that Odysseus is a great hero (metis, endurance, his relationships) and the case that his flaws undermine this (hubris, ruthlessness, the deaths of his crew). Reach a clear, supported conclusion — sitting on the fence is not a judgement.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Odysseus’s heroism rests on metis (cunning intelligence), karteria (endurance) and his devotion to kleos and time; he is defined by intelligence rather than strength, making him a different kind of hero from Achilles.
  • His key flaws are hubris (excessive pride, shown when he reveals his name to Polyphemus) and a capacity for ruthless deception; these complicate but do not cancel his heroic status.
  • Athena favours Odysseus precisely because he shares her defining quality — metis — and she intervenes at every critical moment to support his mission; his relationship with her is one of intellectual equals.

practice_questions.text: Name the Greek term for the lasting glory or fame a hero wins through great deeds.
Describe two qualities that Homer presents as central to Odysseus's heroism in the Odyssey.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two qualities, up to a maximum of 3 with one development. Acceptable qualities: metis / cunning intelligence (e.g. the Nobody trick in Book 9); endurance / karteria (e.g. enduring seven years on Calypso's island without giving up; sitting disguised as a beggar in his own palace); devotion to his family and home (refusing immortality from Calypso); oratorical skill / ability to tell his own story (Books 9–12). 1 mark for development of either quality with a specific example.

practice_questions.text:
Read this paraphrase of a moment from Book 9 of the Odyssey:

'His ships were far from the shore and out of danger. Then Odysseus called back to the Cyclops: "Cyclops! If any mortal man ever asks you who put out your ugly eye, tell them it was Odysseus, son of Laertes, who lives in Ithaca!" His men begged him to stop — every instinct told them to stay silent — but he would not listen.'

What does this passage reveal about the flaws of Odysseus as a hero? Use specific details from the passage in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses at least two specific details with developed explanation. Likely points: 'his ships were far from shore and out of danger' — the timing makes the boast an act of pure vanity, not necessity; Odysseus reveals his name and address — undoing the anonymity that saved his life, showing that pride (hubris) defeats his own intelligence; 'his men begged him to stop' — the crew's instinct is right; their fear shows this is a failure of judgement; 'he would not listen' — the inability to suppress his need for recognition is the defining flaw that costs him Poseidon's enmity. Candidates who link specific details to the theme of hubris and its consequences score more highly.
Secure: Two details identified and explained.
Developing: One detail explained clearly.
Emerging: General comment about Odysseus being too proud with little textual reference.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Odysseus's relationship with the goddess Athena contributes to his success in the Odyssey.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Athena is Odysseus's divine protector — she favours him because he shares her quality of metis (cunning intelligence). 1 mark for: a specific act of help (e.g. she gives him his beggar's disguise when he arrives in Ithaca; she appeals to Zeus to secure his release from Calypso; she tips the battle in Book 22). 1 mark for: the significance — her patronage ensures divine sanction for Odysseus's mission. 1 mark for: the deeper point — their relationship shows that intelligence is not just a human virtue but a divine one, and Homer uses this to elevate metis to the highest heroic value.

practice_questions.text: 'Odysseus's flaws make him a less admirable hero than his qualities suggest.' How far do you agree? Refer to specific episodes from the Odyssey to support your judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained argument that weighs qualities against flaws across multiple episodes. For agreement: hubris in Book 9 (revealing his name) destroys his crew's safety and earns Poseidon's enmity — a single act of pride undoes much of what his cleverness achieved; his ruthlessness (killing all suitors without exception; the punishment of the maidservants) raises moral questions; he lies even to loyal characters. Against: his metis achieves what bie alone could not (Polyphemus, Circe, the suitors); his endurance (refusing Calypso's immortality, sitting as a beggar in his own hall) shows extraordinary self-control; his devotion to home over divine status is presented as admirable. A top answer will note that Homer does not resolve this tension simply — the poem invites the reader to hold the qualities and flaws simultaneously. Supported judgement required.
Secure: At least two episodes discussed with relevant analysis; judgement reached.
Developing: Mostly one side; limited evidence.
Emerging: General discussion of Odysseus without specific episodes.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between metis and bie as heroic values in the Odyssey, using specific examples from the prescribed books.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed explanation of both terms with at least two contrasting examples. Metis: cunning / indirect action (Nobody trick; disguise; Hermes / moly in Book 10; patience in Books 19–22). Bie: raw physical force (associated with Achilles in the Iliad; Polyphemus represents bie — massive but easily outwitted; the suitors' numerical strength is irrelevant against Odysseus's strategy). The key point is that the Odyssey argues metis is more valuable because the challenges of the homecoming cannot be solved by strength alone — only by intelligence, self-restraint and cunning.
Secure: Both terms explained with at least one example each.
Developing: One term explained clearly; the other mentioned but undeveloped.
Emerging: General reference to Odysseus being clever without explaining the contrast.

knowledge_checks.q: What does the Greek word 'kleos' mean in the context of Homeric epic?
options: Honour or respect from one's community
Lasting glory or fame won through great deeds

knowledge_checks.q: Why does Athena favour Odysseus above other mortals, according to the Odyssey?
options: He is the strongest warrior in Greece
He sacrifices to her more than any other god
He shares her defining quality of metis — cunning intelligence

knowledge_checks.q: Odysseus refuses the goddess Calypso's offer of immortality because he would rather be mortal and return to his wife and _____.
The Greek word for Odysseus's quality of steadfast endurance and ability to bear suffering is _____.
Match each Greek heroic concept to its meaning:
right: Lasting glory or fame that survives a hero's death in poetry
Honour — the respect and recognition owed to a hero by his community
Excessive pride that violates divine boundaries and invites punishment

flashcard_questions.q: What is kleos in Homeric epic?
flashcard_questions.a: The lasting fame a hero wins through great deeds, which lives on in song after his death.

flashcard_questions.q: What is time in the Homeric world?
flashcard_questions.a: Honour — the respect and recognition owed to a hero by his community and peers.

flashcard_questions.q: What Greek quality does Odysseus demonstrate when he refuses immortality from Calypso?
flashcard_questions.a: Endurance (karteria) — he chooses a mortal life with his family over divine status.

flashcard_questions.q: What is hubris, and how does it cause Odysseus problems in Book 9?
flashcard_questions.a: Excessive pride; he boasts his real name to Polyphemus, earning Poseidon's enmity.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Greek word 'karteria' mean?
flashcard_questions.a: Steadfast endurance — the ability to bear suffering patiently without giving up.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'bie' mean as a heroic quality, and who best represents it in Homeric epic?
flashcard_questions.a: Raw physical strength; best represented by Achilles in the Iliad.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Athena admire Odysseus above other mortals?
flashcard_questions.a: He shares her defining quality of metis — cunning intelligence.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the Odyssey show Odysseus's role as a father?
flashcard_questions.a: His return inspires Telemachus to grow from a passive boy into a man who fights alongside him.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Odysseus's greatest failure as a leader in the Odyssey?
flashcard_questions.a: He cannot prevent his crew from eating the cattle of Helios, causing their destruction.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the Odyssey contrast Odysseus with Achilles as heroic types?
flashcard_questions.a: Achilles embodies bie (strength and immediate action); Odysseus embodies metis (cunning and patience).

flashcard_questions.q: In the Odyssey, what does Odysseus's endurance while disguised as a beggar in his own hall reveal?
flashcard_questions.a: His extraordinary self-control — he waits for the right moment rather than acting on impulse.

glossary_terms.definition: The Greek word for glory or fame won through great deeds; a hero's kleos lives on after his death in the songs of poets.
The Greek word for honour; the recognition and respect that a hero was owed by his community and peers.
In the Greek tradition, an arrogance or excessive pride that leads a person to violate the boundaries set by the gods, inviting divine punishment.
A Greek quality of steadfast endurance, the ability to bear suffering and hardship with patience and determination; one of Odysseus's most admired traits.
